module_title: Agrarian Succession, Declaratory Suits & Revenue Recovery
introduction: Tailored for Judicial Service Mains, this level explores the complex, highly specific mechanics of agricultural succession (which famously overrides personal laws), the eviction of trespassers from public utility land, and the draconian coercive processes used by the State to recover unpaid land revenue.

core_concepts.title: Succession of Agricultural Land (Devolution)
core_concepts.description:
A massive jurisprudential exception: The devolution of agricultural tenancy is governed strictly by the State Revenue Codes, **NOT by the Hindu Succession Act or Muslim Personal Law**.
- UP Code (Sec 108): It provides a strict, gender-neutral statutory order of succession for all religions to prevent the fragmentation of agricultural holdings. 
- The Hierarchy: (a) Widow, unmarried daughters, and male lineal descendants per stirpes. (b) Mother and Father. (c) Married daughters. (The 2006 Code progressively elevated unmarried daughters to inherit simultaneously with sons).

core_concepts.title: Declaratory Suits (Section 144, UP Code)
core_concepts.description:
When a person's title or right as a Bhumidhar or Asami is disputed, they must file a 'Declaratory Suit'. 
- Jurisdiction: This suit is filed in the Revenue Court (Assistant Collector / SDO), NOT a Civil Court. The court examines evidence and officially declares the plaintiff's status as the lawful tenure holder, ordering the Khatauni to be corrected accordingly.

core_concepts.title: Eviction from Gram Panchayat Land (Section 67, UP Code)
core_concepts.description:
Protection of public utility lands (Pastures, Ponds, Graveyards).
- The Mechanism: If any person encroaches upon or illegally occupies land belonging to the Gram Panchayat or local authority, the Assistant Collector can issue a show-cause notice. 
- The Order: Upon proof of trespass, the court will order immediate eviction, demolition of the illegal structure, and impose a heavy fine as compensation for wrongful occupation.

core_concepts.title: Coercive Recovery of Land Revenue Arrears
core_concepts.description:
Land revenue is the 'first charge' on the land. If a farmer defaults, the State has draconian powers to recover it (Sec 170 UP Code / Sec 147 MPLRC):
1. Issue of Citation / Demand Notice.
2. Arrest and detention of the defaulter.
3. Attachment and sale of the defaulter's movable property (tractors, bank accounts).
4. Attachment of the specific holding (land) for which the arrear is due.
5. Sale/Auction of the holding itself to recover the dues.

important_entities.name: Escheat (Section 115, UP Code)
important_entities.key_fact: When the State inherits the land.
important_entities.significance: If a Bhumidhar or Asami dies intestate (without a Will) and leaves absolutely no legal heirs recognized under the statutory hierarchy of succession, the land does not sit abandoned. By the doctrine of Escheat, the land automatically vests in the State Government.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Advanced exams test the limitations on coercive recovery. Can the Tahsildar arrest a pregnant female farmer who defaults on land revenue? **NO**. Under the UP Revenue Code, women, minors, and senior citizens (typically above 65 years) are expressly **exempted** from arrest and detention for the recovery of land revenue arrears.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember the logical escalation of coercive processes: start with a warning, restrict liberty, seize tractors/bank accounts, and only as a last resort, auction the land itself.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Law Optional or State Judiciary Mains, when analyzing gender justice in property law, highlight the evolution of **Section 108 of the UP Revenue Code**, noting how it overrides religious personal laws to provide uniform, agrarian-specific succession that now grants parity to unmarried daughters.
